briefdescription.para: The blend weight of the manifold-based mass lumping scheme.

detaileddescription.para:
rowSumsHighOrder
Row sums of the consistent mass matrix built from the element's own (high-order) shape functions, i.e. the integral of each $N_i$ over the element.
rowSumsLinear
Row sums built from the linear (corner-node) shape functions of the same element, one entry per corner node.
The blend weight $w$ to use in $\hat{N} = w\,N + (1-w)\,N_\mathrm{lin}$.
The scheme is manifold-based lumping:

listitem.para: Yang, Y., Zheng, H. & Sivaselvan, M. V. (2017). "A rigorous and unified mass lumping scheme for higher-order elements". CMAME 319, 491-514. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2017.03.011
Duczek, S. & Gravenkamp, H. (2019). "Critical assessment of different mass lumping schemes for higher order serendipity finite elements". CMAME 350, 836-897. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2019.03.028

detaileddescription.para: It row-sums a blended shape function $\hat{N} = w N + (1-w) N_\mathrm{lin}$. Row-summing $N$ alone is not positive for a serendipity element its corner shape functions integrate to a negative value and blending in the linear shape functions is what restores positivity.

The weight cannot be a constant, which is the subtlety this function exists for. A corner node's lumped mass is $w S^{N}_i + (1-w) S^{\mathrm{lin}}_i$, so with $S^{N}_i < 0 < S^{\mathrm{lin}}_i$ positivity requires \[ w < w_\mathrm{max} = \min_i \frac{S^{\mathrm{lin}}_i}{S^{\mathrm{lin}}_i - S^{N}_i}. \] That limit is element-dependent, because the corner row sum is:

A hard-coded $w = \tfrac{1}{2}$ therefore sits comfortably inside the admissible range in 2D and exactly on its boundary in 3D, where it produces corner masses of exactly zero a singular lumped mass matrix, and one that lands a few 1e-17 either side of zero in floating point rather than on it, so an "is any mass zero" check downstream passes and the inverse mass comes out around 1e17.

Returned here is $w = \min(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{2}{3} w_\mathrm{max})$. The $\tfrac{2}{3}$ is a safety fraction chosen here rather than taken from either reference, but it is not free-floating: it is the largest simple fraction that still yields $w = \tfrac{1}{2}$ for quad8, and the values it produces are the published ones on both element types where a published value exists

listitem.para: $w = \tfrac{1}{2}$ for quad8, the split of Yang et al. (2017),
$w = \tfrac{1}{3}$ for hexa20, the split assessed by Duczek & Gravenkamp (2019),

detaileddescription.para: so the rule is not merely a way of staying off the positivity boundary; it reproduces the literature wherever the literature has an answer, and extrapolates in the same spirit where it does not. The cap keeps $\tfrac{1}{2}$ as the value used wherever it is safe.

An element with no negatively-integrating corner shape function (every linear element, since there $N_\mathrm{lin} \equiv N$ and the result does not depend on $w$ at all) is unconstrained and gets $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

simplesect.para: The reproduction of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ for quad8 is exact analytically, not necessarily bit-exact: the row sums are accumulated numerically over the element's own quadrature points, so $w_\mathrm{max}$ can land an ulp below $\tfrac{3}{4}$ (it does for a quad8 under 2x2 reduced integration) and the returned weight then sits an ulp below $\tfrac{1}{2}$ rather than on it. The difference is far below any tolerance the lumped masses are checked against, but it is a rounding-level difference and not a bitwise identity.

Positivity is enforced at the corner nodes only, which is all a blend weight can reach. A node with no linear counterpart carries $w S^{N}_i$, so if its own shape function integrates to a negative value not possible for any of the element types in use, but reachable in principle by a sufficiently distorted one its lumped mass is negative for every $w > 0$ and this function cannot help. A positive returned weight is therefore not a guarantee of a positive definite lumped mass matrix.

briefdescription.para: The per-node lumped mass fractions of the manifold-based scheme, summing to one.

detaileddescription.para:
rowSumsHighOrder
Row sums from the element's own shape functions.
rowSumsLinear
Row sums from the linear shape functions, one per corner node.
weight
The blend weight, from manifoldBlendWeight().
One fraction per node, summing to one.
Density-free on purpose: positivity and the mass distribution are properties of the element geometry and its shape functions, so the same fractions serve the lumped mass (scaled by density) and the critical time step (which needs only the distribution). Sharing them is what keeps the two from drifting apart a time step derived from a different mass distribution than the one actually assembled is exactly the sort of inconsistency that shows up as an unexplained instability.

Note the total is independent of the weight: the blend moves mass between the corner and the remaining nodes but conserves the element total. That is why an incorrect weight leaves the element mass, and hence the model mass, perfectly correct and is invisible to any check that looks at totals.

simplesect.para: Integrating the blended shape function once, as done here and by the callers, is exactly equivalent to assembling the blended consistent mass matrix $M = \int \hat{N}^T \hat{N} \rho \,dV$ and row-summing that the form in which the scheme is usually written and implemented. Both $N$ and $N_\mathrm{lin}$ are partitions of unity and the blend is convex, so $\sum_j \hat{N}_j \equiv 1$ and \[ \sum_j M_{ij} = \int \hat{N}_i \Big( \sum_j \hat{N}_j \Big) \rho \,dV = \int \hat{N}_i \rho \,dV. \] The linear form is therefore not an approximation of the quadratic one; it is the same numbers at a fraction of the cost, and no consistent mass matrix has to be formed to get them.

The normalisation is skipped, and the raw blended row sums returned, if their total is not positive. That cannot happen for any element whose geometry is valid, since the total is the element volume; it is a guard against dividing by a degenerate element's zero volume, not a supported mode.

briefdescription.para: The factor by which a non-uniform lumped mass tightens the critical time step.

detaileddescription.para:
massFractions
Per-node lumped mass fractions, from manifoldMassFractions().
The factor to apply to a characteristic-length / wave-speed time step estimate.
The usual estimate $\Delta t = l / c$ is the stable increment for an element whose mass is spread uniformly over its nodes, each carrying $1/n$ of it. Lumping does not spread it uniformly, and the lightest node sets the highest frequency: $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$, so the stable increment scales with $\sqrt{m_\mathrm{min} / m_\mathrm{uniform}}$, which is what is returned.

Exactly 1 for a linear element on a regular mesh, slightly below 1 for a distorted one (correct: a distorted element does have a tighter limit than its volume alone suggests), and 0.913 for a hexa20 under this scheme.

simplesect.para: This corrects only the mass-distribution part of the estimate. It does NOT correct for polynomial order, and that residue is large: a convergence study on a GC3D20R bar shows the answer settling only around a courant number of 0.1-0.2, i.e. roughly a further factor of five unaccounted for, because $l/c$ is a linear-element formula and a quadratic element's highest free eigenfrequency is well above what it predicts. Closing that properly wants an eigenvalue-based estimate rather than another factor.

A non-positive smallest fraction returns 1.0, i.e. the uncorrected $l/c$ estimate. That is deliberately a fallback and not a fix: a non-positive nodal mass means the lumping itself has failed, no time step derived from it is meaningful, and no blend weight can repair it (see the second

on manifoldBlendWeight()). Scaling $l/c$ by $\sqrt{m_\mathrm{min}/m_\mathrm{uniform}}$ would return zero or NaN and mask the cause, so the estimate is left alone and the assembled mass is where the failure belongs.

Nothing currently reports it there either: the only check on the assembled lumped mass is on the solver side and tests for an exact zero, which a negative or near-zero nodal mass passes. So a lumping failure is at present silent in both places. Detecting it at assembly is the right fix and is deliberately out of scope here.
